principle: Every record carries the time it BECAME AVAILABLE, and the service consumes records in that order. A record that arrives late is applied late. Nothing may be delivered before the moment it could have existed.

ordering.rule: strictly non-decreasing available_at within a stream
ordering.batch_note: fixed: Block 8's link memory updates once per batch, so batch size IS the memory staleness the models were trained with. Changing it is a train/serve mismatch.

messages.name: event
messages.available_at: t_first_packet + 0.010 s, or flow end if earlier
messages.required: ALWAYS. Without it the flow is never scored.
messages.note: the 10 ms verdict. Carries only packets seen by then.

fields.event_id: int64, unique within the day, monotonic in t
fields.t: float64 epoch seconds, the flow's first packet
fields.sender_ip: string, the host that sent the flow's FIRST packet
fields.reversed: bool, true when the flow record's src/dst disagree with first-packet direction
fields.dt_src: float32 seconds since this sender's previous event, -1 if none
fields.dt_dst: float32 seconds since this receiver's previous event, -1 if none
fields.port_delta: float32, destination port minus the sender's previous destination port
fields.dst_port_new: float32 in {0,1}, 1 if this sender has not used this destination port before
fields.has_packets: bool; a flow with no captured packets is dropped, not scored
fields.n_pkt: int16, packets seen by t_obs, capped at 20
fields.pkt: float32[20][13] per-packet features in this exact order: ['length', 'ttl', 'tcp_window', 'tcp_flag_syn', 'tcp_flag_ack', 'tcp_flag_fin', 'tcp_flag_rst', 'tcp_flag_psh', 'tcp_flag_urg', 'payload_len', 'tcp_retransmission', 'frag', 'direction']
fields.dt: float32[20] seconds since the flow's previous packet, zero-padded after n_pkt
fields.node_id_warning: sender_node_id/receiver_node_id are keyed on the flow's FIRST CAPTURED PACKET. events.parquet also carries src_node_id/dst_node_id keyed on the flow RECORD, and the two disagree on 11.2-33.5% of rows depending on the day. Block 8's links use sender/receiver. Never mix them.

messages.name: packet_summary
messages.available_at: time of the flow's 20th captured packet
messages.required: CONDITIONAL: required whenever the served Block 8 checkpoint has flow_messages=True - which every checkpoint we have trained does. Omitting it does not crash, but it is a TRAIN/SERVE MISMATCH: in training the summary arrived for essentially every flow (98.6% of Bot events, after the verdict), so 'no summary ever arrived' is a state the model never saw.
messages.note: the flow's own aggregate over its first 20 packets. Arrives after the verdict for most flows: measured 98.6% of Bot events (median 2 ms later) and 97.0% of DoS-Hulk (median 127 ms).

fields.event_id: int64, the event this belongs to
fields.summary_note: 20 columns, not 15. Derived from the flow's first 20 packets. iat_mean is the mean of the K-1 gaps, so the summary's own availability time is t + iat_mean * max(pkt_n - 1, 0).

messages.name: flow_record
messages.required: CONDITIONAL: required whenever the served Block 8 checkpoint has flow_records=True. With flow_records=False it is ignored entirely and computing it is wasted work.
messages.note: the full CICFlowMeter record. Measured median 106 s AFTER the verdict (91.3% of DoS-Slowloris flows late). Must never reach the 10 ms verdict of its own flow. Three data faults to handle: direction is keyed to the record's own Src IP and disagrees with first-packet direction on 11.2-33.5% of rows depending on the day (swap the 22 Fwd/Bwd pairs and set record_reversed); Active/Idle columns hold epoch timestamps, not durations, and are excluded; rate columns contain infinities and must be sanitised.

fields.available_at: float64 epoch seconds, the flow's close
fields.record: float32[69] = the 68 CICFlowMeter columns minus Active/Idle, plus record_reversed. Exact order in models.context_encoder.records.RECORD_COLUMNS.
fields.record_reversed: bool, true if the Fwd/Bwd pairs were swapped to match first-packet direction

verdicts.note: a SEPARATE observation with its own time. Never fold it back into the observation stage.

anticipation.note: horizon is in EVENTS, not seconds: 20 events on a sender key spans a median 16 s but 0.36 s at the 10th percentile. Report the wall-clock lead beside it.

incidents.rule: alerts on one key with no quiet gap longer than gap_seconds collapse into one incident
incidents.note: this is what an operator counts. Measured: 30 alert events became 8 incidents on the world model, 27 on the detection head.

threshold.source: the serve_threshold field of the head checkpoint (models/detector/head.py --save), written there by models/evaluation/thresholds.py. Nothing else writes that field, and a threshold from a different fit is meaningless rather than merely wrong
threshold.note: thresholds do not survive retraining; they are model-version scoped. Carry threshold_id in every verdict.

persistence.reset_on: any event on that key below threshold
persistence.measured: halves false alarms (58 -> 30) at zero cost to early recall or campaign onsets

operating_point.correction_2026_09_20: recall_early and onsets_caught_early here were measured on the 3M-event Bot slice. attack_slice centres on the attack span: on the Bot day it starts 3,446 s AFTER the first Bot attack and contains 0 of the day's 1,239,249 pre-attack rows. So those two figures describe mid-campaign detection, not anticipation, and 'onsets' are attack resumptions rather than campaign starts. false_alarms_per_hour and precision are unaffected in kind but are slice-conditioned and need one full-day confirmation
operating_point.arm: WORLD MODEL (Block 10), sender-keyed, Bot day slice. `recall_early` and `onsets_caught_early` exist only in this arm, so these figures are not detector numbers.

detection_arm_equivalent.note: the arm shipping first. Same emitter rules, different score scale, so different thresholds and rates.
detection_arm_equivalent.funnel: 16,240 above threshold -> 15,406 after persist-3 -> 21 incidents; all 10 attacking hosts alerted

implemented_in.use: AlertEmitter(threshold, persist=3, gap=60.0, capacity=500_000); push(key, score, t) -> incident dict or None; push_batch(keys, scores, times) -> list of incidents
implemented_in.was: all three stages existed only as whole-file offline scripts (tools/world_model/fpr_levers.py, tools/world_model/alert_economics.py). They are now incremental, which is what a live process needs
implemented_in.ordering: push order IS availability order. A run of three means three CONSECUTIVE events on that key, so feeding a batch sorted by anything else changes the answer
implemented_in.key_hygiene: the emitter prunes keys whose incident closed more than one gap ago, and hard-drops the oldest half if that frees nothing, so the table stays bounded without losing an open incident
implemented_in.counters: rates(hours) returns events, alerts, incidents and both per-hour rates -- these are what GET /health should expose
implemented_in.performance: push_batch compares the whole batch in one torch kernel and moves only the rows that clear the threshold to the host. At a 0.003% budget that is 99.997% of the batch never touched by Python. Push order must still be availability order

recalibration.use: Recalibrator(budget, span=200_000, recent=50_000, tolerance=3.0); observe(benign_scores); threshold(); drifted(realised_rate) -> bool
recalibration.why_two_samples: a threshold read from one contiguous recent stretch overshot its budget SIX-FOLD on another segment of the same day. So it keeps a reservoir sample spanning everything seen PLUS a FIFO of the most recent rows, and reads the quantile off their union
recalibration.what_to_feed: scores of rows that did not alert. Circular but conservative: an attack that slips under the threshold drags the threshold down, never up
recalibration.when_to_recalibrate: whenever drifted() is true -- the realised rate is outside 3x of the budget either way. Offline the quantile rule held between 1.0x and 2.4x across five orders of magnitude, so beyond 3x is outside anything measured

alert_emission.what_transfers_between_arms: The RULES transfer: persistence and incident aggregation are decision rules over a score stream and their multipliers hold for either arm. The RATES do not: they depend on the score distribution, the threshold and the benign population. Never quote 41.9/hour for the detector or 8.4/hour for the world model.

state_limits.lru_note: Block 8 has no cap yet and needs one. Measured on Block 10: capping at 25% of keys with 237,028 evictions left recall identical to four decimals, because the median sender host has 7 lifetime events.

block8_link_memory.status: DONE -- this was Kaustuk's, not yours
block8_link_memory.api: ContextEncoder(..., capacity=N) or begin_day(n_links, capacity=N); below 1 it is a fraction of the stream's links
block8_link_memory.travels: the value is stored in the Block 8 checkpoint, so block9.frozen_block8 and models/detector/head.py --block8 honour it automatically
block8_link_memory.default: None, which keeps one row per link -- every existing checkpoint is provably unaffected
block8_link_memory.measured: 1,000 distinct links through a 250-slot table produced 750 evictions; on Block 10's equivalent table, 25% of keys with 237,028 evictions gave identical recall to four decimals

throughput.measurement_note: offline, fed from parquet; excludes ingest and event construction
throughput.cpu_only: UNMEASURED - an earlier benchmark silently used the GPU

from_the_capture_pipeline.live packet/flow feed: your own source. Must yield, per flow: the first 20 packets with per-packet features, the side counters, and the CICFlowMeter record at flow close.

model_artefacts_required.data/model_cache/context/<run>/best.pt: Block 8, frozen. Holds link memory; carries arm, flow_messages, flow_records flags in the checkpoint.
model_artefacts_required.data/model_cache/block9/<run>/best.pt: Block 9, frozen. Produces z and recon_error.
model_artefacts_required.the detection head checkpoint: the supervised multi-class classifier. Produced by models/detector/head.py.
model_artefacts_required.a thresholds file: per family and per observation_population, scoped to a model version. DOES NOT EXIST YET - see 'recalibration' in docs/yug.md; you and Kaustuk need to agree its format.
model_artefacts_required.Block 7 checkpoint \u2014 OPEN ITEM, DOE: Every Block 7 checkpoint on disk is a leave-one-day-out EXPERIMENT artefact, named '<train days>__<held-out day>__a_pkt__gnn__relu__s<seed>.pt' under data/model_cache/scores/<variant>/. None is trained on all days, so none is the one to serve. The flow_embeddings manifest records only the encoder CONFIG (variant a_pkt, packet_encoder gnn, k_packets 20, mode online_prefix, budget_ms 10.0, side split, 65,000 parameters) and names no checkpoint. A live deployment needs a Block 7 trained on all days - that is on Kaustuk's side and is part of the full 5-day training run. Until it exists, serving would have to pick an arbitrary held-out-day checkpoint, which is not a defensible choice.

reference_data_required.data/events/<day>/node_index.parquet: node_id -> ip. You need the reverse direction live: assign a stable node_id to each IP, and decide what happens for an IP never seen before (it must get a fresh id and a cold state).
reference_data_required.data/context_features/<day>/side_feature: reference for the exact side-counter definitions your live path must reproduce.

config_that_must_match_training.why: batch size IS the memory staleness the models were trained with; TTL and budget are baked into the checkpoints

open_items_blocking_you: a thresholds file format, agreed with Kaustuk
the LRU cap is now implemented in Block 8 (models/context_encoder/model.py, LinkMemory.reset(n_links, capacity)) - pass a capacity when you serve

FLOW_CLOSE VERDICT - a second, separate observation

the flow_close verdict overwriting or amending the observation verdict - they are separate rows

required_means.the_field_answers: is this message needed for the system to behave AS MEASURED - not merely whether it crashes without it. Those are different questions and conflating them was an error in v1.0 of this contract.
required_means.will_it_crash_without_it: No, for kinds 2 and 3. Block 8's link memory merges kinds by UNION: each kind has its own slot and a PRESENCE BIT, so 'nothing of this kind arrived' is representable. Nothing errors.
required_means.will_it_be_correct_without_it: NO, if the served checkpoint expects that kind. Every Block 8 we trained has flow_messages=True, and in training the summary arrived for essentially every flow. Serving without kind 2 means every link permanently reads a state that never occurred during training, and results will drift from the measured numbers with nothing to signal it.
required_means.HOW TO DECIDE: read the flags off the checkpoint, do not choose: s = torch.load('<block8>/best.pt', map_location='cpu', weights_only=False); send kind 2 iff s['flow_messages'], send kind 3 iff s['flow_records']. Current checkpoints: f_norec_s0 = {flow_messages: True, flow_records: False}; f_rec_s0 = {flow_messages: True, flow_records: True}.
required_means.absent_vs_late: a LATE message is normal and correct - apply it at its availability time, never before. A PERMANENTLY ABSENT kind that the checkpoint expects is a configuration error, not a tolerated condition.
required_means.what_optional_really_meant: only that the wire protocol tolerates absence without erroring. It never meant you may choose not to send it.

who_consumes_what.note: Both optional message kinds ARE consumed - just in different blocks, at different times, and in the 20-packet case with different CONTENT each time. This is the part most likely to be implemented wrongly.

consumer_1.CONTENT: the aggregate over packets available BY 10 ms - a PREFIX, not the full 20. Same 20 columns, different numbers.
consumer_1.also: it is one of Block 7's reconstruction targets (recon_targets: a, pkt, a_future)

consumer_2.who: Block 8 link memory, as MESSAGE KIND 2
consumer_2.when: at flow_time = t + iat_mean * max(pkt_n - 1, 0), i.e. when the 20th packet lands
consumer_2.why_it_is_new_information: Block 7 only saw the prefix, so the completed aggregate carries something it could not have known. Measured: it lands after the verdict for 98.6% of Bot events (median 2 ms later) and 97.0% of DoS-Hulk (median 127 ms), but 0.0% of DoS-SlowHTTPTest, whose packets all fall inside the budget.

the_20_packet_aggregate.so: you must send it as its own timestamped message even though Block 7 already consumed a version of it. They are not the same data.

consumer_1.who: population tagging - NOT a model input
consumer_1.code: models/data/inputs.py: 'x_f is never a model input; observe() reads its Flow Duration only to tag the population'; models/data/prefix.py reads X_COLUMNS.index('Flow Duration')
consumer_1.LIVE NOTE: offline this is derived from the record's Flow Duration. LIVE you do not need the record for it - you already know whether the flow was still open at t+10 ms. Same semantics, cheaper source. Tag the population directly and do not wait on the record.

consumer_2.who: Block 8 link memory, as MESSAGE KIND 3
consumer_2.when: at record_time, the flow's close - a median 106 s after the verdict

consumer_3.what_for: logistic regression on all 69 columns, the floor the system is measured against. Not part of serving.

consumer_4.what_for: run 7's late-fusion arm, which lost. Not part of serving.

WHO_BENEFITS.note: The record enters at ONE point - Block 8, message kind 3 - but Block 8's context feeds BOTH arms. So it reaches the world model through Block 8, not separately. What differs is who benefits.
WHO_BENEFITS.world model / anticipation: HELPS. Sender-key false alarms 6,111-8,200 -> 5,686-5,702 (disjoint across seeds), next-state skill 0.276-0.290 -> 0.300-0.303, and the seed-to-seed spread collapses from 2,089 false alarms to 16.
WHO_BENEFITS.supervised / detection: HURTS. False alarms at 99% recall 1-2 -> 2-4; PR-AUC on completed_before_budget 0.9995 -> 0.9986-0.9991.
WHO_BENEFITS.THE DECISION: one Block 8 serves both arms, so you cannot have records for anticipation and not for detection without running TWO Block 8 instances - doubling link-memory state and compute. Three options: (a) two instances, (b) one WITH records and accept slightly worse detection, (c) one WITHOUT and accept slightly worse anticipation. This is Kaustuk's call, not a serving default.

summary_table: AGG_COLUMNS prefix   -> Block 7 input            -> at 10 ms
AGG_COLUMNS full     -> Block 8 message kind 2   -> at the 20th packet
record Flow Duration -> population tag           -> live: derive it yourself, do not wait for the record
record 69 columns    -> Block 8 message kind 3   -> at flow close, +106 s median, only if flow_records=True

how_to_calculate.test_window_hours: hours = (max(t_obs[test]) - min(t_obs[test])) / 3600. On the Bot 3M slice this is 0.715 h. Every per-hour figure divides by it, so quote it beside any rate.
how_to_calculate.recall: TP / (TP + FN) over TEST rows only, where a positive is an event whose target is true.
how_to_calculate.recall_early: TP_early / P_early, where P_early = TEST rows that are BENIGN and have an attack coming on their key within H. This is the anticipation number. On the Bot sender key P_early = 320.
how_to_calculate.recall_ongoing: TP_ongoing / P_ongoing over TEST rows that are THEMSELVES attacks with more attack following. P_ongoing = 16,379, so pooled recall is 98% this number - never report recall alone.
how_to_calculate.fpr: FP / N_negatives over TEST rows. N_negatives = 558,522 on the Bot 3M slice.
how_to_calculate.false_incidents_per_hour: collapse alerts first, then divide. Collapse = group alerts by key, sort by time, and start a new incident whenever the gap to the previous alert on that key exceeds gap_seconds. An incident is TRUE if ANY alert inside it was a true positive, FALSE otherwise. Example: 30 alerts -> 8 false incidents -> 8 / 0.715 = 11.2/hour. The gap is a choice with a real cost: 1.81x collapse at 10 s, 3.42x at 60 s, 5.91x at 300 s.
how_to_calculate.onsets_caught_early: count of campaign ONSETS in test that had an alert fire strictly before them. An onset is the first attack event of a campaign on a key - its first attack, or the first after a benign gap. Each campaign contributes exactly one, so unlike recall_early this cannot be inflated by one long campaign. Bot sender key: 291 onsets in test.
how_to_calculate.lead_events / lead_seconds: for each alert that precedes an attack on its key: lead_events = the number of events between them; lead_seconds = t_obs(attack) - t_obs(alert). Report the MEDIAN and p90 of both. Measured: 1 event and 2.02 s at BOTH median and p90.
how_to_calculate.probability_within_H: from the rollout, per family f: P(f within H) = 1 - prod over k=1..H of (1 - p_k[f]), where p_k = softmax(head(state after k imagined steps)). Compute in log space: 1 - exp(sum_k log(1 - p_k[f])) - the direct product underflows.
how_to_calculate.ece: Expected Calibration Error. Bin predictions by predicted probability (15 bins). In each bin b compute |mean(predicted) - fraction(actually happened)|. ECE = sum_b (n_b / N) * that gap. 0 is perfect. Read it as: at ECE 0.002, a stated 3% happens 3% +/- 0.2 percentage points of the time.
how_to_calculate.brier: mean((predicted probability - outcome)^2) over TEST rows. Lower is better; it penalises both miscalibration and poor discrimination, where ECE sees only miscalibration.
how_to_calculate.next_state_skill_vs_persistence: 1 - MSE(model) / MSE(persistence), where persistence predicts z_next = z_now on the same key. 0 = no better than assuming nothing changes; 1 = perfect; NEGATIVE = worse than doing nothing, which is what a broken design looks like. Always report the persistence MSE beside it - a raw MSE means nothing alone.
how_to_calculate.persistence_rule (persist-k): alert only when k CONSECUTIVE events on the same key exceed the threshold. Keep a counter per key; increment on an event above threshold, RESET TO ZERO on any event below it; fire when the counter reaches k. Measured at k=3: false alarms 58 -> 30 with recall_early and onsets unchanged.
how_to_calculate.threshold_from_budget: threshold = quantile(scores of CALIBRATION rows that are negative, 1 - budget). Calibration rows are validation only by default - measured better than validation+train on this data (1.112% vs 1.300% realised against a 1% budget) because splits are time-ordered and validation sits nearest test.
how_to_calculate.threshold_from_precision_floor: walk the precision-recall curve on calibration rows and take the HIGHEST-RECALL threshold whose precision reaches the floor. Equivalent in outcome to a budget but stated in terms an operator can agree to. Measured: precision>=0.999 landed on the same point as a 3e-5 budget.

definitions_from_code.end: t + Flow Duration, i.e. the flow's LAST packet
definitions_from_code.t_obs: min(t + 0.010, end) - models/data/prefix.py. The verdict moment. A flow that finishes inside the budget is scored when it finishes, not at t+10 ms.
definitions_from_code.observation_population: COMPLETED if end <= t + 0.010, else EARLY - same file, same line
definitions_from_code.flow_time (kind 2): t + iat_mean * max(pkt_n - 1, 0) - models/context_encoder/data.py. The moment the K-th packet lands, derived because exporting exact per-packet times would mean re-reading every packet of every day. Checked against real packet times on 200,000 events: median difference 0.2 ns, worst 8.3 us, which is float32 in the stored aggregates.
definitions_from_code.record_time (kind 3): t + Flow Duration - models/context_encoder/records.py. This is the EARLIEST the record can exist, not when it is emitted.

CORRECTION_records_are_not_always_late.the_error: earlier versions of this contract said the record arrives 'a median 106 s after the verdict' as if always. It does not.
CORRECTION_records_are_not_always_late.why: record_time == end, and for a COMPLETED_BEFORE_BUDGET flow t_obs == end too - so the record's earliest existence time EQUALS the verdict time for those flows.

measured_on_Thursday_15.Benign: 54.9% of records land after the verdict, median lag 2.2 s, p90 115.9 s

CORRECTION_records_are_not_always_late.so: roughly 45% of benign records are available at the verdict moment. The 106 s figure is the median lag among SLOWLORIS records that are late - the worst case, not the typical one.

timing_and_availability.LIVE_emission_time: record_time is a floor. CICFlowMeter emits at flow close or at its idle/active timeout, which is at or after t + Flow Duration. Stamp kind 3 with YOUR ACTUAL emission time and deliver in that order. Do not back-date it to t + Flow Duration - that would claim the record existed before you had it.
timing_and_availability.the_rule_that_still_holds: a flow's own kind-3 record must never inform that flow's own 10 ms verdict. Block 8 queues messages and applies them at the START of the next batch, so a record whose availability time equals t_obs reaches memory one batch later and cannot affect its own event. Preserve that: queue, then apply on the next batch boundary.
timing_and_availability.two_verdicts: stage='observation' at t_obs, and stage='flow_close' when the record lands. For a completed_before_budget flow these can be close together or simultaneous in time, but they are still two separate rows with their own timestamps.

statistics_you_must_report.why: these are the numbers that tell us whether the live path matches the measured system. Report them per run.
statistics_you_must_report.throughput_events_per_second: count events processed / wall seconds. Ours offline is 18,000-20,000/s EXCLUDING ingest and event construction. Yours includes them, so expect lower - report both your end-to-end figure and, if you can, the model-only figure.
statistics_you_must_report.peak_load_handled: the highest sustained events/s before the queue grows. Peak in the data is ~3,200/s.
statistics_you_must_report.per_event_latency_ms: t_emit - t_obs, median and p99. The budget is 10 ms to the verdict; anything you add on top is lead time lost.
statistics_you_must_report.state_keys_resident: rows currently held in Block 8's link memory and Block 10's table.
statistics_you_must_report.evictions_total: cumulative LRU evictions. Ours: 237,028 at a 25% cap with recall unchanged to four decimals. A far higher rate than that is a sign the cap is too small.
statistics_you_must_report.messages_dropped_or_late: count kind-2 and kind-3 messages that arrived after their link had already been evicted, or that you could not deliver. This is the number that silently degrades results, and nothing else will reveal it.
statistics_you_must_report.alerts_and_incidents_per_hour: false alarms / test hours, and false INCIDENTS / test hours after collapsing by key with gap_seconds. Target at the recommended operating point: ~42 alerts/hour and ~11 incidents/hour.
statistics_you_must_report.population_split: fraction of flows tagged early_observation vs completed_before_budget. Ours on the Bot slice: 370,705 vs 187,799 benign. A large drift here means your budget or flow-end detection differs from ours.
statistics_you_must_report.cpu_only_throughput: run once with the GPU disabled. NEVER VALIDLY MEASURED on our side - an earlier benchmark silently used the GPU, so there is no number to compare against yet.

lead_time_the_truth.headline: The ~2 second lead is a property of the TARGET DEFINITION, not of the model or the training objective. Measured 2026-09-20 as ground truth, with no model involved.
lead_time_the_truth.what_was_measured: for every benign TEST event on a host that ever attacks, the unbounded time until that host's next attack - no horizon cap at all
lead_time_the_truth.therefore: the maximum warning available ANYWHERE in this data on the sender key is 2.0 seconds. No training objective can produce lead the data does not contain.
lead_time_the_truth.why_the_data_is_like_this: an attacking host emits 2,582 events/hour against a median host's 1.9, so its benign traffic is interleaved with its attack traffic at sub-second spacing. 'A benign event on an attacking host' is almost by definition adjacent to an attack. A target phrased as 'attack within H EVENTS on this key' can therefore never span more than a couple of seconds on a busy host.
lead_time_the_truth.what_we_tried_and_abandoned: a lead-rewarding objective (--lead-steps: roll the dynamics forward during training and supervise each rolled step against the class at that distance). Implemented and tested, then ABANDONED once the ground-truth measurement above showed there is nothing for it to learn. The flag remains in models/world_model_proxy/model.py; it is not a defect, it simply cannot help on this target.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CREATE LEAD.PRINCIPLE: the rollout predicts STATE -> NEXT STATE. A step is one more event on the key, not a tick of a clock. PREDICT in state transitions; REPORT in seconds. Reporting lead_seconds beside lead_events is right and necessary for an operator; phrasing the TARGET in seconds is not, because it would force the rollout to additionally predict inter-event gaps - a different and harder model that breaks the transition framing.
WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CREATE LEAD.rejected_time_based_horizon: 'attack within T SECONDS on this key' was proposed and WITHDRAWN. It asks the rollout to answer in units it does not operate in. Keep the horizon in events.

still_open_campaign_level.target: will this host attack at all - the state of a host BEFORE it has ever attacked
still_open_campaign_level.why_it_stays_state_shaped: still per-event, still 'what comes next'. Only the label changes.
still_open_campaign_level.the_lead_it_could_offer: whatever traffic precedes a host's FIRST attack. Unmeasured until now - the 2.0 s ceiling was measured on benign events that have a LATER attack, which is a different population from events before the first one.

still_open_cross_host.target: host A is attacking - is host B next
still_open_cross_host.why_it_stays_state_shaped: it is a GRAPH rollout, not a time one: the state of A conditioning the state of B. Block 8 already carries that structure - per-link memory plus neighbourhood attention over recent peers - so the machinery exists.
still_open_cross_host.the_lead_it_could_offer: the stagger between hosts' first attacks. Topology being a star does NOT rule this out - that conflates topology with timing. If the 10 Bot hosts start at staggered times, the stagger is real lead regardless of them all hitting one hub.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CREATE LEAD.why_the_2s_ceiling_is_not_a_units_proble: on an attacking host, benign traffic does not precede attacks by much - measured max 2.0 s unbounded. Re-expressing the same target in seconds cannot create positives that do not exist. The lead has to come from a DIFFERENT KEY or a DIFFERENT POINT IN THE CAMPAIGN.

lead_time_the_truth.correction_note: earlier versions of these documents called the lead 'the biggest capability gap' and told the Block 10 owner to fix the objective. That was wrong and would have wasted his time. The gap is real but it is a TARGET design question, and on this dataset it may be unanswerable.

runtime.default: reproducible: cudnn.benchmark off, cudnn.deterministic on, TF32 off
runtime.fast: configure(fast=True) enables cuDNN autotuning and TF32. Both change results in the last bits, so do not enable them on a process whose thresholds were calibrated without them
